e-612.knowledge_point: Finding the Antiderivative of a Vector-Valued Function
e-612.problem: Find $\mathbf F(t)$ given that $\mathbf F'(t)= \langle 6t^5+2t, \sec^2 t\rangle.$
e-612.worked_solution:
Note that 

$$
\mathbf F(t)=\int \mathbf F'(t)\, \textrm d t=\int \left\langle 6t^5+2t,\, \sec^2 t\right\rangle \, \textrm d t.
$$

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨6{t}^{5}+2t,\,{sec}^{2}⁡t⟩\,\text{d}t & =⟨\int (6{t}^{5}+2t)\,\text{d}t,\,\int {sec}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{6}+{t}^{2}+{c}_{1},\,\operatorname{tan}⁡t+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{6}+{t}^{2},\,\operatorname{tan}⁡t⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{6}+{t}^{2},\,\operatorname{tan}⁡t⟩+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $\mathbf C$ is an arbitrary (vector) constant of integration.

e-613.worked_solution:
To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+1),\,4⟩\,\text{d}t=⟨\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+1)\,\text{d}t,\,\int 4\,\text{d}t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

- For $x(t) =\cos(2t+1),$ we calculate its integral using substitution. So, we let $u= 2t +1.$ Then

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d t} = 2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm d t = \dfrac 1 2 \textrm d u.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+1)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡u\cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \operatorname{cos}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡u)+{c}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+1)+{c}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

- For $y(t) =4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int y(t)\,\text{d}t=\int 4\text{d}t=4t+{c}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+1),\,4⟩\,\text{d}t & =⟨\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+1)+{c}_{1},\,4t+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+1),\,4t⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+1),\,4t⟩+C.\end{aligned}
$$

e-615.knowledge_point: Finding the Antiderivative of a Vector-Valued Function That Satisfies a Given Initial Condition
e-615.problem: Calculate $\mathbf F(t)$ given that $\mathbf F'(t)= \left\langle \sec t \tan t, \,  \sin(2t)\right\rangle$ and $\mathbf F(0)=\langle 0,\, 0\rangle.$
e-615.worked_solution:
Note that 

$$
\mathbf F(t)=\int \mathbf F'(t)\, \textrm d t=\int \left\langle \sec t \tan t,\,  \sin(2t)\right\rangle \, \textrm d t.
$$

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨\operatorname{sec}⁡t\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)⟩\,\text{d}t & =⟨\int \operatorname{sec}⁡t\operatorname{tan}⁡t\,\text{d}t,\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{sec}⁡t+{c}_{1},\,-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+{c}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

The initial condition $\mathbf F(0)=\left\langle 0,\, 0 \right\rangle$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}F(0)=⟨\operatorname{sec}⁡0+{c}_{1},\,-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot 0)+{c}_{2}⟩ & =⟨0,\,0⟩ \\ ⟨1+{c}_{1},\,-\frac{1}{2}+{c}_{2}⟩ & =⟨0,\,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $c_1=-1$ and $c_2=\dfrac 12.$ Consequently, 

$$
\mathbf F(t)=\left\langle  \sec t - 1  , \,  -\dfrac 1 2\cos(2t)+ \dfrac12\right\rangle.
$$

after.worked_solution:
First, we note that 

$$
F(t)=\int {F}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t=\int ⟨3{t}^{2}-5,\,\frac{1}{t}⟩\text{d}t.
$$

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨3{t}^{2}-5,\,\frac{1}{t}⟩\text{d}t & =⟨\int (3{t}^{2}-5)\,\text{d}t,\int \frac{1}{t}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{3}-5t+{c}_{1},\,\operatorname{ln}⁡|t|+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{3}-5t,\,\operatorname{ln}⁡|t|⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{3}-5t,\,\operatorname{ln}⁡|t|⟩+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary (vector) constant of integration.

after.html:
Question 1
?

If F′(t)=⟨3t2−5,1t⟩, then F(t)=

a
⟨t3−5,ln⁡|t|⟩+C
b
⟨t3−5t,−1t2⟩+C
c
⟨6t,−1t2⟩+C
d
⟨6t,ln⁡|t|⟩+C
e
⟨t3−5t,ln⁡|t|⟩+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we note that F(t)=∫F′(t)dt=∫⟨3t2−5,1t⟩dt.

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we get

∫⟨3t2−5,1t⟩dt=⟨∫(3t2−5)dt,∫1tdt⟩=⟨t3−5t+c1,ln⁡|t|+c2⟩=⟨t3−5t,ln⁡|t|⟩+⟨c1,c2⟩=⟨t3−5t,ln⁡|t|⟩+C,

where C is an arbitrary (vector) constant of integration.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Antiderivative of a Vector-Valued Function
content.worked_solution:
First, we note that 

$$
F(t)=\int {F}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t=\int ⟨3{t}^{2}-5,\,\frac{1}{t}⟩\text{d}t.
$$

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨3{t}^{2}-5,\,\frac{1}{t}⟩\text{d}t & =⟨\int (3{t}^{2}-5)\,\text{d}t,\int \frac{1}{t}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{3}-5t+{c}_{1},\,\operatorname{ln}⁡|t|+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{3}-5t,\,\operatorname{ln}⁡|t|⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{3}-5t,\,\operatorname{ln}⁡|t|⟩+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary (vector) constant of integration.

Question 2
?

If F′(t)=⟨sec⁡ttan⁡t,−sin⁡t⟩, then F(t)=

a
⟨sec⁡ttan⁡t,−cos⁡t⟩+C
b
⟨−csc⁡t,cos⁡t⟩+C
c
⟨csc⁡t,cos⁡t⟩+C
d
⟨sec⁡t,cos⁡t⟩+C
e
⟨sec⁡t,−cos⁡t⟩+C
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrate each component: the antiderivative of sec(t)tan(t) is sec(t), and the antiderivative of −sin(t) is cos(t). Thus F(t)=⟨sec(t), cos(t)⟩+C, where C is an arbitrary constant vector.

after.name: Question 2
after.worked_solution:
First, we note that 

$$
F(t)=\int {F}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t=\int ⟨\operatorname{sec}⁡t\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\text{d}t.
$$

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨\operatorname{sec}⁡t\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\text{d}t & =⟨\int \operatorname{sec}⁡t\operatorname{tan}⁡t\,\text{d}t,-\int \operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{sec}⁡t+{c}_{1},\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{sec}⁡t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{sec}⁡t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary (vector) constant of integration.

Question 2
?

If F′(t)=⟨sec⁡ttan⁡t,−sin⁡t⟩, then F(t)=

a
⟨sec⁡ttan⁡t,−cos⁡t⟩+C
b
⟨−csc⁡t,cos⁡t⟩+C
c
⟨csc⁡t,cos⁡t⟩+C
d
⟨sec⁡t,cos⁡t⟩+C
e
⟨sec⁡t,−cos⁡t⟩+C
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we note that F(t)=∫F′(t)dt=∫⟨sec⁡ttan⁡t,−sin⁡t⟩dt.

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we get

∫⟨sec⁡ttan⁡t,−sin⁡t⟩dt=⟨∫sec⁡ttan⁡tdt,−∫sin⁡tdt⟩=⟨sec⁡t+c1,cos⁡t+c2⟩=⟨sec⁡t,cos⁡t⟩+⟨c1,c2⟩=⟨sec⁡t,cos⁡t⟩+C,

where C is an arbitrary (vector) constant of integration.

verification.explanation: The revealed solution confirms option d. Differentiating ⟨sec(t), cos(t)⟩+C gives ⟨sec(t)tan(t), −sin(t)⟩, exactly the stated derivative. The incorrect submission selected option a.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Antiderivative of a Vector-Valued Function
content.worked_solution:
First, we note that 

$$
F(t)=\int {F}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t=\int ⟨\operatorname{sec}⁡t\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\text{d}t.
$$

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨\operatorname{sec}⁡t\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\text{d}t & =⟨\int \operatorname{sec}⁡t\operatorname{tan}⁡t\,\text{d}t,-\int \operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{sec}⁡t+{c}_{1},\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{sec}⁡t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{sec}⁡t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary (vector) constant of integration.

before.html:
Question 3
?

If F′(t)=⟨csc2⁡t,cos⁡t⟩, then F(t)=

a
⟨−sin⁡t,−cos⁡t⟩+C
b
⟨−cot⁡t,cos⁡t⟩+C
c
⟨−cot⁡t,sin⁡t⟩+C
d
⟨cot⁡t,−sin⁡t⟩+C
e
⟨tan⁡t,sin⁡t⟩+C
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating componentwise gives ∫csc²(t) dt = −cot(t) and ∫cos(t) dt = sin(t). Thus F(t)=⟨−cot(t), sin(t)⟩+C, which is option c.

after.name: Question 3
after.worked_solution:
First, we note that 

$$
F(t)=\int {F}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t=\int ⟨{csc}^{2}⁡t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\text{d}t.
$$

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨{csc}^{2}⁡t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\text{d}t & =⟨\int {csc}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t,\int \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{cot}⁡t+{c}_{1},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{cot}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{cot}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary (vector) constant of integration.

after.worked_solution:
First, we note that 

$$
F(t)=\int {F}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t=\int ⟨{csc}^{2}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\text{d}t.
$$

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨{csc}^{2}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\text{d}t & =⟨\int {csc}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t,\int (\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{cot}⁡t+{c}_{1},\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{cot}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{cot}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩+C,\end{aligned}
$$

 

where $C$ is an arbitrary (vector) constant of integration.

Question 4
?

If F′(t)=⟨csc2⁡t,sin⁡t⟩, then F(t)=

a
⟨−cot⁡t,−cos⁡t⟩+C
b
⟨−cot⁡(2t),sin2⁡t⟩+C
c
⟨−cot⁡t,cos2⁡t⟩+C
d
⟨−csc⁡t,−cos⁡t⟩+C
e
⟨−tan⁡t,−cos⁡t⟩+C
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we note that F(t)=∫F′(t)dt=∫⟨csc2⁡t,sin⁡t⟩dt.

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we get

∫⟨csc2⁡t,sin⁡t⟩dt=⟨∫csc2⁡tdt,∫(sin⁡t)dt⟩=⟨−cot⁡t+c1,−cos⁡t+c2⟩=⟨−cot⁡t,−cos⁡t⟩+⟨c1,c2⟩=⟨−cot⁡t,−cos⁡t⟩+C,

where C is an arbitrary (vector) constant of integration.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms option a: differentiating −cot(t) gives csc²(t), and differentiating −cos(t) gives sin(t). The deliberately incorrect submission selected option b.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Antiderivative of a Vector-Valued Function
content.worked_solution:
First, we note that 

$$
F(t)=\int {F}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t=\int ⟨{csc}^{2}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\text{d}t.
$$

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨{csc}^{2}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\text{d}t & =⟨\int {csc}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t,\int (\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{cot}⁡t+{c}_{1},\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{cot}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{cot}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩+C,\end{aligned}
$$

 

where $C$ is an arbitrary (vector) constant of integration.

If F′(t)=⟨1,cos⁡t+2t⟩, then F(t)=

a
⟨1+t,sin⁡t+2t2⟩+C
b
⟨t,cos⁡t+t⟩+C
c
⟨t2,sin⁡t+t2⟩+C
d
⟨t,sin⁡t+t2⟩+C
e
⟨t2,cos⁡t⟩+C
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating componentwise, ∫1 dt = t and ∫(cos(t)+2t) dt = sin(t)+t². Adding an arbitrary constant vector C gives option d.

after.name: Question 5
after.worked_solution:
First, we note that 

$$
F(t)=\int {F}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t=\int ⟨1,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2t⟩\text{d}t.
$$

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨1,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2t⟩\text{d}t & =⟨\int 1\,\text{d}t,\,\int (\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2t)\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨t+{c}_{1},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{t}^{2}+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{t}^{2}⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{t}^{2}⟩+C,\end{aligned}
$$

 

where $C$ is an arbitrary (vector) constant of integration.

where C is an arbitrary (vector) constant of integration.

\begin{aligned}\int ⟨1,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2t⟩\text{d}t & =⟨\int 1\,\text{d}t,\,\int (\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2t)\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨t+{c}_{1},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{t}^{2}+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{t}^{2}⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{t}^{2}⟩+C,\end{aligned}
$$

 

where $C$ is an arbitrary (vector) constant of integration.

after.worked_solution:
To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨{3}^{t},\,{csc}^{2}⁡t⟩\text{d}t & =⟨\int {3}^{t}\,\text{d}t,\int {csc}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{{3}^{t}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}+{c}_{1},\,-\operatorname{cot}⁡t+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{{3}^{t}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3},\,-\operatorname{cot}⁡t⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{{3}^{t}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3},\,-\operatorname{cot}⁡t⟩+C\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately: ∫⟨3t,csc2⁡t⟩dt=⟨∫3tdt,∫csc2⁡tdt⟩=⟨3tln⁡3+c1,−cot⁡t+c2⟩=⟨3tln⁡3,−cot⁡t⟩+⟨c1,c2⟩=⟨3tln⁡3,−cot⁡t⟩+C

verification.explanation: The revealed solution confirms option a. Differentiating 3^t/ln(3) gives 3^t, and differentiating −cot(t) gives csc²(t). The deliberately incorrect submission selected option b.

content.knowledge_point: Integrating a Vector-Valued Function
content.worked_solution:
To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨{3}^{t},\,{csc}^{2}⁡t⟩\text{d}t & =⟨\int {3}^{t}\,\text{d}t,\int {csc}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{{3}^{t}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}+{c}_{1},\,-\operatorname{cot}⁡t+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{{3}^{t}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3},\,-\operatorname{cot}⁡t⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{{3}^{t}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3},\,-\operatorname{cot}⁡t⟩+C\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 7
?

Find ∫⟨sec⁡ttan⁡t,6te(t2−1)⟩dt.

a
⟨tan⁡t,6tet2−1⟩+C
b
⟨tan⁡t,3et2−1⟩+C
c
⟨sec⁡t,3et2−1⟩+C
d
⟨sec⁡t,3tet2−1⟩+C
e
⟨sec⁡t,2tet2−1⟩+C
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrate componentwise: ∫sec(t)tan(t) dt = sec(t). For the second component, let u=t²−1, so du=2t dt and ∫6t e^(t²−1) dt = 3e^(t²−1). Thus option c is correct.

after.name: Question 7
after.worked_solution:
To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨\operatorname{sec}⁡t\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,6t{e}^{({t}^{2}-1)}⟩\,\text{d}t=⟨\int \operatorname{sec}⁡t\operatorname{tan}⁡t\,\text{d}t,\,\int 6t{e}^{({t}^{2}-1)}\,\text{d}t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

- For $x(t)=\operatorname{sec}⁡t\operatorname{tan}⁡t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x(t)\,\text{d}t=\int \operatorname{sec}⁡t\operatorname{tan}⁡t\,\text{d}t=\operatorname{sec}⁡t+{c}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

- For $y(t)=6t{e}^{({t}^{2}-1)},$ we calculate its integral using substitution. So, we let $u={t}^{2}-1.$ Then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t}=2t\,⟹\,\text{d}t=\frac{1}{2t}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,  we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int y(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int 6t{e}^{({t}^{2}-1)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int 6t{e}^{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2t}\,\text{d}u \\  & =3\int {e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =3{e}^{u}+{c}_{2} \\  & =3{e}^{{t}^{2}-1}+{c}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨\operatorname{sec}⁡t\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,6t{e}^{({t}^{2}-1)}⟩\,\text{d}t & =⟨\operatorname{sec}⁡t+{c}_{1},\,3{e}^{{t}^{2}-1}+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{sec}⁡t,\,3{e}^{{t}^{2}-1}⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{sec}⁡t,\,3{e}^{{t}^{2}-1}⟩+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Find ∫⟨sec⁡ttan⁡t,6te(t2−1)⟩dt.

a
⟨tan⁡t,6tet2−1⟩+C
b
⟨tan⁡t,3et2−1⟩+C
c
⟨sec⁡t,3et2−1⟩+C
d
⟨sec⁡t,3tet2−1⟩+C
e
⟨sec⁡t,2tet2−1⟩+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately:

∫⟨sec⁡ttan⁡t,6te(t2−1)⟩dt=⟨∫sec⁡ttan⁡tdt,∫6te(t2−1)dt⟩.

  • For x(t)=sec⁡ttan⁡t, we have ∫x(t)dt=∫sec⁡ttan⁡tdt=sec⁡t+c1.
  • For y(t)=6te(t2−1), we calculate its integral using substitution. So, we let u=t2−1. Then
    dudt=2t⟹dt=12tdu. Therefore, we have ∫y(t)dt=∫6te(t2−1)dt=∫6teu⋅12tdu=3∫eudu=3eu+c2=3et2−1+c2.

Finally, we get

∫⟨sec⁡ttan⁡t,6te(t2−1)⟩dt=⟨sec⁡t+c1,3et2−1+c2⟩=⟨sec⁡t,3et2−1⟩+⟨c1,c2⟩=⟨sec⁡t,3et2−1⟩+C.

content.knowledge_point: Integrating a Vector-Valued Function
content.worked_solution:
To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨\operatorname{sec}⁡t\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,6t{e}^{({t}^{2}-1)}⟩\,\text{d}t=⟨\int \operatorname{sec}⁡t\operatorname{tan}⁡t\,\text{d}t,\,\int 6t{e}^{({t}^{2}-1)}\,\text{d}t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

- For $x(t)=\operatorname{sec}⁡t\operatorname{tan}⁡t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x(t)\,\text{d}t=\int \operatorname{sec}⁡t\operatorname{tan}⁡t\,\text{d}t=\operatorname{sec}⁡t+{c}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

- For $y(t)=6t{e}^{({t}^{2}-1)},$ we calculate its integral using substitution. So, we let $u={t}^{2}-1.$ Then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t}=2t\,⟹\,\text{d}t=\frac{1}{2t}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,  we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int y(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int 6t{e}^{({t}^{2}-1)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int 6t{e}^{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2t}\,\text{d}u \\  & =3\int {e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =3{e}^{u}+{c}_{2} \\  & =3{e}^{{t}^{2}-1}+{c}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨\operatorname{sec}⁡t\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,6t{e}^{({t}^{2}-1)}⟩\,\text{d}t & =⟨\operatorname{sec}⁡t+{c}_{1},\,3{e}^{{t}^{2}-1}+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{sec}⁡t,\,3{e}^{{t}^{2}-1}⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{sec}⁡t,\,3{e}^{{t}^{2}-1}⟩+C.\end{aligned}
$$

b

c

e
⟨sin⁡t,3e(2t+1)2⟩+C

decision.explanation: Integrate each component: ∫cos(t) dt = sin(t), and ∫3e^(2t+1) dt = (3/2)e^(2t+1), since the exponent has derivative 2. Adding a constant vector C gives option e.

after.name: Question 8
after.worked_solution:
To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,2{e}^{(2t+1)}⟩\,\text{d}t=⟨\int \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t,\,\int 2{e}^{(2t+1)}\,\text{d}t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

- For $x(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x(t)\,\text{d}t=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t=\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{c}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

- For $y(t)=2{e}^{(2t+1)},$ we calculate its integral using substitution. So, we let $u=2t+1.$ Then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t}=2\,⟹\,\text{d}t=\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,  we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int y(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int 2{e}^{(2t+1)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int 3{e}^{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\int {e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{e}^{u}+{c}_{2} \\  & =\frac{3{e}^{(2t+1)}}{2}+{c}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,3{e}^{(2t+1)}⟩\,\text{d}t & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{c}_{1},\,\frac{3{e}^{(2t+1)}}{2}+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\frac{3{e}^{(2t+1)}}{2}⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\frac{3{e}^{(2t+1)}}{2}⟩+C.\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Integrating a Vector-Valued Function
content.worked_solution:
To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,2{e}^{(2t+1)}⟩\,\text{d}t=⟨\int \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t,\,\int 2{e}^{(2t+1)}\,\text{d}t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

- For $x(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x(t)\,\text{d}t=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t=\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{c}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

- For $y(t)=2{e}^{(2t+1)},$ we calculate its integral using substitution. So, we let $u=2t+1.$ Then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t}=2\,⟹\,\text{d}t=\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,  we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int y(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int 2{e}^{(2t+1)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int 3{e}^{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\int {e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{e}^{u}+{c}_{2} \\  & =\frac{3{e}^{(2t+1)}}{2}+{c}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,3{e}^{(2t+1)}⟩\,\text{d}t & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{c}_{1},\,\frac{3{e}^{(2t+1)}}{2}+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\frac{3{e}^{(2t+1)}}{2}⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\frac{3{e}^{(2t+1)}}{2}⟩+C.\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨\frac{3}{t},\,\frac{5}{{t}^{2}}⟩\,\text{d}t & =⟨\int \frac{3}{t}\,\text{d}t,\,\int \frac{5}{{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨3\operatorname{ln}⁡|t|+{c}_{1},\,-\frac{5}{t}+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨3\operatorname{ln}⁡|t|,\,-\frac{5}{t}⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨3\operatorname{ln}⁡|t|,\,-\frac{5}{t}⟩+C\end{aligned}
$$

Find ∫⟨3t,5t2⟩dt.

a
−⟨3ln⁡|t|,5t⟩+C
b
⟨ln⁡|t|,1t⟩+C
c
⟨ln⁡|t|,−5t⟩+C
d
⟨3ln⁡|t|,5t⟩+C
e
⟨3ln⁡|t|,−5t⟩+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately:

∫⟨3t,5t2⟩dt=⟨∫3tdt,∫5t2dt⟩=⟨3ln⁡|t|+c1,−5t+c2⟩=⟨3ln⁡|t|,−5t⟩+⟨c1,c2⟩=⟨3ln⁡|t|,−5t⟩+C

content.knowledge_point: Integrating a Vector-Valued Function
content.worked_solution:
To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨\frac{3}{t},\,\frac{5}{{t}^{2}}⟩\,\text{d}t & =⟨\int \frac{3}{t}\,\text{d}t,\,\int \frac{5}{{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨3\operatorname{ln}⁡|t|+{c}_{1},\,-\frac{5}{t}+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨3\operatorname{ln}⁡|t|,\,-\frac{5}{t}⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨3\operatorname{ln}⁡|t|,\,-\frac{5}{t}⟩+C\end{aligned}
$$

Question 10
?

Find ∫⟨et,10cos⁡(2t−π6)⟩dt.

a
⟨et−1,5sin⁡(2t−π6)⟩+C
b
⟨et,5sin⁡(2t−π6)⟩+C
c
⟨et,5sin⁡(2t)⟩+C
d
⟨et−1,sin⁡(t−π6)⟩+C
e
⟨e5t,5cos⁡(t−π2)⟩+C
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrate componentwise: ∫e^t dt = e^t, and ∫10cos(2t−π/6) dt = 5sin(2t−π/6), accounting for the inner derivative 2. Thus option b is correct.

after.name: Question 10
after.worked_solution:
To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨{e}^{t},\,10\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t-\frac{\pi }{6})⟩\text{d}t=⟨\int {e}^{t}\,\text{d}t,\,\int 10\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t-\frac{\pi }{6})\,\text{d}t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

- For $x(t)={e}^{t},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x(t)\,\text{d}t=\int {e}^{t}\text{d}t={e}^{t}+{c}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

- For $y(t)=10\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t-\frac{\pi }{6}),$ we calculate its integral using substitution. So, we let $u=2t-\frac{\pi }{6}.$ Then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t}=2\,⟹\,\text{d}t=\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,  we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int y(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int 10\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t-\frac{\pi }{6})\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int 10\operatorname{cos}⁡u\cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{10}{2}\int \operatorname{cos}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =5(\operatorname{sin}⁡u)+{c}_{2} \\  & =5\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t-\frac{\pi }{6})+{c}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨{e}^{t},\,10\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t-\frac{\pi }{6})⟩\text{d}t & =⟨{e}^{t}+{c}_{1},\,5\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t-\frac{\pi }{6})+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{t},\,5\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t-\frac{\pi }{6})⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{t},\,5\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t-\frac{\pi }{6})⟩+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Find ∫⟨et,10cos⁡(2t−π6)⟩dt.

a
⟨et−1,5sin⁡(2t−π6)⟩+C
b
⟨et,5sin⁡(2t−π6)⟩+C
c
⟨et,5sin⁡(2t)⟩+C
d
⟨et−1,sin⁡(t−π6)⟩+C
e
⟨e5t,5cos⁡(t−π2)⟩+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately:

∫⟨et,10cos⁡(2t−π6)⟩dt=⟨∫etdt,∫10cos⁡(2t−π6)dt⟩.

  • For x(t)=et, we have ∫x(t)dt=∫etdt=et+c1.

  • For y(t)=10cos⁡(2t−π6), we calculate its integral using substitution. So, we let u=2t−π6. Then
    dudt=2⟹dt=12du. Therefore, we have ∫y(t)dt=∫10cos⁡(2t−π6)dt=∫10cos⁡u⋅12du=102∫cos⁡udu=5(sin⁡u)+c2=5sin⁡(2t−π6)+c2.

Finally, we get

∫⟨et,10cos⁡(2t−π6)⟩dt=⟨et+c1,5sin⁡(2t−π6)+c2⟩=⟨et,5sin⁡(2t−π6)⟩+⟨c1,c2⟩=⟨et,5sin⁡(2t−π6)⟩+C.

content.knowledge_point: Integrating a Vector-Valued Function
content.worked_solution:
To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨{e}^{t},\,10\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t-\frac{\pi }{6})⟩\text{d}t=⟨\int {e}^{t}\,\text{d}t,\,\int 10\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t-\frac{\pi }{6})\,\text{d}t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

- For $x(t)={e}^{t},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x(t)\,\text{d}t=\int {e}^{t}\text{d}t={e}^{t}+{c}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

- For $y(t)=10\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t-\frac{\pi }{6}),$ we calculate its integral using substitution. So, we let $u=2t-\frac{\pi }{6}.$ Then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t}=2\,⟹\,\text{d}t=\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,  we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int y(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int 10\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t-\frac{\pi }{6})\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int 10\operatorname{cos}⁡u\cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{10}{2}\int \operatorname{cos}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =5(\operatorname{sin}⁡u)+{c}_{2} \\  & =5\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t-\frac{\pi }{6})+{c}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨{e}^{t},\,10\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t-\frac{\pi }{6})⟩\text{d}t & =⟨{e}^{t}+{c}_{1},\,5\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t-\frac{\pi }{6})+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{t},\,5\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t-\frac{\pi }{6})⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{t},\,5\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t-\frac{\pi }{6})⟩+C.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: The first component has antiderivative ln|1−cot(t)|, giving ln(2)−ln(1)=ln(2). The second gives [2sin(t)] from π/2 to 3π/4 = √2−2. Thus option e is correct.

after.name: Question 12
after.worked_solution:
To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4}⟨\frac{{csc}^{2}⁡t}{1-\operatorname{cot}⁡t},\,2\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\,\text{d}t & =⟨{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4}\frac{{csc}^{2}⁡t}{1-\operatorname{cot}⁡t}\,\text{d}t,{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4}2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\operatorname{cot}⁡t){|}_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4},\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡t{|}_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4}⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{4}))-\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})),\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{4})-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡2-\operatorname{ln}⁡1,\,\sqrt{2}-2⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡2,\,\sqrt{2}-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 14
after.worked_solution:
To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each componentt separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{4}⟨2t-1,\,\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}⟩\text{d}t & =⟨{\int }_{1}^{4}(2t-1)\,\text{d}t,{\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨({t}^{2}-t)\,\,{|}_{1}^{4},\,\sqrt{t}\,\,{|}_{1}^{4}\,\,⟩ \\  & =⟨\text{ }({4}^{2}-4)-({1}^{2}-1),\,\sqrt{4}-\sqrt{1}⟩ \\  & =⟨12,\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Integrate componentwise: [√t]₁⁹ = 3−1 = 2, and [t]₁⁹ = 9−1 = 8. Thus option e is correct.

after.name: Question 15
after.worked_solution:
To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each componentt separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{9}⟨\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}},\,1⟩\text{d}t & =⟨{\int }_{1}^{9}\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}\,\text{d}t,{\int }_{1}^{9}1\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\sqrt{t}\,\,{|}_{1}^{9},\,t\,\,{|}_{1}^{9}⟩ \\  & =⟨\sqrt{9}-\sqrt{1},\,9-1⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\,8⟩\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 16
?

If F′(t)=⟨20t3,16t(t2−1)⟩ and F(1)=⟨1,5⟩, then F(t)=

a
⟨5t3−5,4(t2−1)2+4⟩
b
⟨5t5−4,4(t−1)2+5⟩
c
⟨5t4+4,4(t2−1)2+5⟩
d
⟨t2−4,4(t4−1)2−5⟩
e
⟨5t4−4,4(t2−1)2+5⟩
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating gives F(t)=⟨5t⁴+c₁, 4(t²−1)²+c₂⟩. The condition F(1)=⟨1,5⟩ gives c₁=−4 and c₂=5, so option e satisfies both requirements.

after.name: Question 16
after.worked_solution:
First, we note that 

$$
F(t)=\int {F}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t=\int ⟨20{t}^{3},\,16t({t}^{2}-1)⟩\text{d}t
$$

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨20{t}^{3},\,16t({t}^{2}-1)⟩\text{d}t & =⟨\int 20{t}^{3}\,\text{d}t,\int 16t({t}^{2}-1)\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨5{t}^{4}+{c}_{1},\,4{({t}^{2}-1)}^{2}+{c}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

  

The initial condition $F(1)=⟨1,\,5⟩$ gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(1)=⟨5\cdot {1}^{4}+{c}_{1},\,4{({1}^{2}-1)}^{2}+{c}_{2}⟩ & =⟨1,\,5⟩ \\ ⟨5+{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ & =⟨1,\,5⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${c}_{1}=-4$ and ${c}_{2}=5.$ Consequently

$$
F(t)=⟨5{t}^{4}-4,\,4{({t}^{2}-1)}^{2}+5⟩.
$$

Question 16
?

If F′(t)=⟨20t3,16t(t2−1)⟩ and F(1)=⟨1,5⟩, then F(t)=

a
⟨5t3−5,4(t2−1)2+4⟩
b
⟨5t5−4,4(t−1)2+5⟩
c
⟨5t4+4,4(t2−1)2+5⟩
d
⟨t2−4,4(t4−1)2−5⟩
e
⟨5t4−4,4(t2−1)2+5⟩
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we note that

F(t)=∫F′(t)dt=∫⟨20t3,16t(t2−1)⟩dt

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we have

∫⟨20t3,16t(t2−1)⟩dt=⟨∫20t3dt,∫16t(t2−1)dt⟩=⟨5t4+c1,4(t2−1)2+c2⟩.

The initial condition F(1)=⟨1,5⟩ gives F(1)=⟨5⋅14+c1,4(12−1)2+c2⟩=⟨1,5⟩⟨5+c1,c2⟩=⟨1,5⟩.

Therefore, c1=−4 and c2=5. Consequently F(t)=⟨5t4−4,4(t2−1)2+5⟩.

verification.explanation: The revealed solution confirms option e. Its derivative is ⟨20t³,16t(t²−1)⟩, and substituting t=1 gives ⟨1,5⟩. The deliberately incorrect submission selected a.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Antiderivative of a Vector-Valued Function That Satisfies a Given Initial Condition
content.worked_solution:
First, we note that 

$$
F(t)=\int {F}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t=\int ⟨20{t}^{3},\,16t({t}^{2}-1)⟩\text{d}t
$$

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨20{t}^{3},\,16t({t}^{2}-1)⟩\text{d}t & =⟨\int 20{t}^{3}\,\text{d}t,\int 16t({t}^{2}-1)\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨5{t}^{4}+{c}_{1},\,4{({t}^{2}-1)}^{2}+{c}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

  

The initial condition $F(1)=⟨1,\,5⟩$ gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(1)=⟨5\cdot {1}^{4}+{c}_{1},\,4{({1}^{2}-1)}^{2}+{c}_{2}⟩ & =⟨1,\,5⟩ \\ ⟨5+{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ & =⟨1,\,5⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${c}_{1}=-4$ and ${c}_{2}=5.$ Consequently

$$
F(t)=⟨5{t}^{4}-4,\,4{({t}^{2}-1)}^{2}+5⟩.
$$

decision.explanation: Integrating componentwise gives ⟨4t^(4/3)+c₁, e^(5t)+c₂⟩. The initial condition gives c₁=2 and 1+c₂=−1, so c₂=−2. Thus option c satisfies both the derivative and initial condition.

after.name: Question 17
after.worked_solution:
First, we note that 

$$
F(t)=\int {F}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t=\int ⟨\frac{16\sqrt[3]{t}}{3},\,5{e}^{5t}⟩\text{d}t.
$$

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨\frac{16\sqrt[3]{t}}{3},\,5{e}^{5t}⟩\,\text{d}t & =⟨\int \frac{16\sqrt[3]{t}}{3}\,\text{d}t,\int 5{e}^{5t}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨4{t}^{4/3}+{c}_{1},\,{e}^{5t}+{c}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

The initial condition $F(0)=⟨2,\,-1⟩$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}F(0)=⟨4\cdot {0}^{4/3}+{c}_{1},\,{e}^{5\cdot 0}+{c}_{2}⟩ & =⟨2,\,-1⟩ \\ ⟨{c}_{1},\,1+{c}_{2}⟩ & =⟨2,\,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${c}_{1}=2$ and ${c}_{2}=-2.$ Consequently

$$
F(t)=⟨4{t}^{4/3}+2,\,{e}^{5t}-2⟩.
$$

a
⟨4t1/3+1,et−1⟩
b
⟨4t4/3−2,e5t−2⟩

Submit

First, we note that

F(t)=∫F′(t)dt=∫⟨16t33,5e5t⟩dt.

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we have

∫⟨16t33,5e5t⟩dt=⟨∫16t33dt,∫5e5tdt⟩=⟨4t4/3+c1,e5t+c2⟩.

The initial condition F(0)=⟨2,−1⟩ gives

F(0)=⟨4⋅04/3+c1,e5⋅0+c2⟩=⟨2,−1⟩⟨c1,1+c2⟩=⟨2,−1⟩.

Therefore, c1=2 and c2=−2. Consequently F(t)=⟨4t4/3+2,e5t−2⟩.

F(0)=⟨4⋅04/3+c1,e5⋅0+c2⟩=⟨2,−1⟩⟨c1,1+c2⟩=⟨2,−1⟩.

Therefore, c1=2 and c2=−2. Consequently F(t)=⟨4t4/3+2,e5t−2⟩.

Question 18

If F′(t)=⟨tan⁡tsec⁡t,2cos⁡(2t)⟩ and F(π)=⟨−3,3⟩, then F(t)=

a
 ⟨sec2⁡t−3,sin⁡(3t)−2⟩
b
 ⟨sec⁡t−2,sin⁡(t)+3⟩
c
⟨sec⁡t−2,sin⁡(2t)+3⟩
d
 ⟨sec⁡(2t)−2,sin⁡(2t)+3⟩
e
⟨sec⁡t+3,sin⁡(2t)−2⟩
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating componentwise gives ⟨sec(t)+c₁, sin(2t)+c₂⟩. Since sec(π)=−1 and sin(2π)=0, the initial condition gives c₁=−2 and c₂=3. Thus option c satisfies both requirements.

after.name: Question 18
after.worked_solution:
First, we note that 

$$
F(t)=\int {F}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t=\int ⟨\operatorname{tan}⁡t\operatorname{sec}⁡t\,,2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)⟩\text{d}t.
$$

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨\operatorname{tan}⁡t\operatorname{sec}⁡t\,,2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)⟩\text{d}t & =⟨\int \operatorname{tan}⁡t\operatorname{sec}⁡t\,\text{d}t,\int 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{sec}⁡t+{c}_{1},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+{c}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

The initial condition $F(\pi )=⟨-3,\,3⟩$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}F(\pi )=⟨\operatorname{sec}⁡(\pi )+{c}_{1},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi )+{c}_{2}⟩ & =⟨-3,\,3⟩ \\ ⟨-1+{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ & =⟨-3,\,3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${c}_{1}=-2$ and ${c}_{2}=3.$ Consequently

$$
F(t)=⟨\operatorname{sec}⁡t-2,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+3⟩.
$$

Question 18
?

If F′(t)=⟨tan⁡tsec⁡t,2cos⁡(2t)⟩ and F(π)=⟨−3,3⟩, then F(t)=

a
 ⟨sec2⁡t−3,sin⁡(3t)−2⟩
b
 ⟨sec⁡t−2,sin⁡(t)+3⟩
c
⟨sec⁡t−2,sin⁡(2t)+3⟩
d
 ⟨sec⁡(2t)−2,sin⁡(2t)+3⟩
e
⟨sec⁡t+3,sin⁡(2t)−2⟩
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we note that

F(t)=∫F′(t)dt=∫⟨tan⁡tsec⁡t,2cos⁡(2t)⟩dt.

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we have

∫⟨tan⁡tsec⁡t,2cos⁡(2t)⟩dt=⟨∫tan⁡tsec⁡tdt,∫2cos⁡(2t)dt⟩=⟨sec⁡t+c1,sin⁡(2t)+c2⟩.

The initial condition F(π)=⟨−3,3⟩ gives

F(π)=⟨sec⁡(π)+c1,sin⁡(2π)+c2⟩=⟨−3,3⟩⟨−1+c1,c2⟩=⟨−3,3⟩.

Therefore, c1=−2 and c2=3. Consequently

F(t)=⟨sec⁡t−2,sin⁡(2t)+3⟩.

verification.explanation: The revealed solution confirms option c. Differentiating gives ⟨tan(t)sec(t), 2cos(2t)⟩, and evaluating at t=π gives ⟨−1−2, 0+3⟩=⟨−3,3⟩. The deliberately incorrect submission selected e.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Antiderivative of a Vector-Valued Function That Satisfies a Given Initial Condition
content.worked_solution:
First, we note that 

$$
F(t)=\int {F}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t=\int ⟨\operatorname{tan}⁡t\operatorname{sec}⁡t\,,2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)⟩\text{d}t.
$$

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨\operatorname{tan}⁡t\operatorname{sec}⁡t\,,2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)⟩\text{d}t & =⟨\int \operatorname{tan}⁡t\operatorname{sec}⁡t\,\text{d}t,\int 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{sec}⁡t+{c}_{1},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+{c}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

The initial condition $F(\pi )=⟨-3,\,3⟩$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}F(\pi )=⟨\operatorname{sec}⁡(\pi )+{c}_{1},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi )+{c}_{2}⟩ & =⟨-3,\,3⟩ \\ ⟨-1+{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ & =⟨-3,\,3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${c}_{1}=-2$ and ${c}_{2}=3.$ Consequently

$$
F(t)=⟨\operatorname{sec}⁡t-2,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+3⟩.
$$

Question 19
?

If F′(t)=⟨2t,2t⟩ and F(1)=⟨1,3⟩, then F(t)=

a
⟨ln⁡(t2)+1,t2−2⟩
b
⟨ln⁡(t2)−1,t2+1⟩
c
⟨ln⁡(t2)−2,t+2⟩
d
⟨ln⁡(t2)+1,t2+2⟩
e
⟨ln⁡t+1,t2+2⟩
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating gives ⟨ln(t²)+c₁, t²+c₂⟩, since ln(t²)=2ln|t| for t≠0. The initial condition gives c₁=1 and c₂=2. Thus option d satisfies both requirements.

after.name: Question 19
after.worked_solution:
First, we note that 

$$
F(t)=\int {F}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t=\int ⟨\frac{2}{t},\,2t⟩\text{d}t.
$$

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨\frac{2}{t},\,2t⟩\,\text{d}t & =⟨\int \frac{2}{t}\,\text{d}t,\int 2t\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨2\operatorname{ln}⁡|t|+{c}_{1},\,{t}^{2}+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡({t}^{2})+{c}_{1},\,{t}^{2}+{c}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

The initial condition $F(1)=⟨1,\,3⟩$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}F(1)=⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡({1}^{2})+{c}_{1},\,(1)^{2}+{c}_{2}⟩ & =⟨1,\,3⟩ \\ ⟨{c}_{1},\,1+{c}_{2}⟩ & =⟨1,\,3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${c}_{1}=1$ and ${c}_{2}=2.$ Consequently

$$
F(t)=⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡({t}^{2})+1,\,{t}^{2}+2⟩.
$$

Question 19
?

If F′(t)=⟨2t,2t⟩ and F(1)=⟨1,3⟩, then F(t)=

a
⟨ln⁡(t2)+1,t2−2⟩
b
⟨ln⁡(t2)−1,t2+1⟩
c
⟨ln⁡(t2)−2,t+2⟩
d
⟨ln⁡(t2)+1,t2+2⟩
e
⟨ln⁡t+1,t2+2⟩
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we note that

F(t)=∫F′(t)dt=∫⟨2t,2t⟩dt.

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we have

∫⟨2t,2t⟩dt=⟨∫2tdt,∫2tdt⟩=⟨2ln⁡|t|+c1,t2+c2⟩=⟨ln⁡(t2)+c1,t2+c2⟩.

The initial condition F(1)=⟨1,3⟩ gives F(1)=⟨ln⁡(12)+c1,(1)2+c2⟩=⟨1,3⟩⟨c1,1+c2⟩=⟨1,3⟩.

Therefore, c1=1 and c2=2. Consequently F(t)=⟨ln⁡(t2)+1,t2+2⟩.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Antiderivative of a Vector-Valued Function That Satisfies a Given Initial Condition
content.worked_solution:
First, we note that 

$$
F(t)=\int {F}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t=\int ⟨\frac{2}{t},\,2t⟩\text{d}t.
$$

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨\frac{2}{t},\,2t⟩\,\text{d}t & =⟨\int \frac{2}{t}\,\text{d}t,\int 2t\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨2\operatorname{ln}⁡|t|+{c}_{1},\,{t}^{2}+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡({t}^{2})+{c}_{1},\,{t}^{2}+{c}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

The initial condition $F(1)=⟨1,\,3⟩$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}F(1)=⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡({1}^{2})+{c}_{1},\,(1)^{2}+{c}_{2}⟩ & =⟨1,\,3⟩ \\ ⟨{c}_{1},\,1+{c}_{2}⟩ & =⟨1,\,3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${c}_{1}=1$ and ${c}_{2}=2.$ Consequently

$$
F(t)=⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡({t}^{2})+1,\,{t}^{2}+2⟩.
$$

Question 20
?

If F′(t)=⟨cos⁡(2t),sec2⁡(t)⟩ and F(π4)=⟨1,0⟩, then F(t)=

a
⟨cos⁡(t)+1,2sec⁡(t)−1⟩
b
⟨12sin⁡(2t)+12,tan⁡(t)⟩
c
⟨12cos⁡(t)−12,2sec⁡(t)+2⟩
d
⟨12sin⁡(2t)+12,tan⁡(t)−1⟩
e
⟨sin⁡(2t)−1,tan⁡(t)−1⟩
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating gives ⟨(1/2)sin(2t)+c₁, tan(t)+c₂⟩. At t=π/4, sin(π/2)=1 and tan(π/4)=1, so c₁=1/2 and c₂=−1. Thus option d satisfies both requirements.

after.name: Question 20
after.worked_solution:
First, we note that 

$$
F(t)=\int {F}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t=\int ⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,,{sec}^{2}⁡(t)⟩\text{d}t.
$$

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,,{sec}^{2}⁡(t)⟩\text{d}t & =⟨\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t,\int {sec}^{2}⁡(t)\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+{c}_{1},\,\operatorname{tan}⁡(t)+{c}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

The initial condition $F(\frac{\pi }{4})=⟨1,\,0⟩$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}F(\frac{\pi }{4})=⟨\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+{c}_{1},\,\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})+{c}_{2}⟩ & =⟨1,\,0⟩ \\ ⟨\frac{1}{2}+{c}_{1},\,1+{c}_{2}⟩ & =⟨1,\,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${c}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}$ and ${c}_{2}=-1.$ Consequently

$$
F(t)=⟨\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+\frac{1}{2},\,\operatorname{tan}⁡(t)-1⟩.
$$

Question 20
?

If F′(t)=⟨cos⁡(2t),sec2⁡(t)⟩ and F(π4)=⟨1,0⟩, then F(t)=

a
⟨cos⁡(t)+1,2sec⁡(t)−1⟩
b
⟨12sin⁡(2t)+12,tan⁡(t)⟩
c
⟨12cos⁡(t)−12,2sec⁡(t)+2⟩
d
⟨12sin⁡(2t)+12,tan⁡(t)−1⟩
e
⟨sin⁡(2t)−1,tan⁡(t)−1⟩
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we note that

F(t)=∫F′(t)dt=∫⟨cos⁡(2t),sec2⁡(t)⟩dt.

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we have

∫⟨cos⁡(2t),sec2⁡(t)⟩dt=⟨∫cos⁡(2t)dt,∫sec2⁡(t)dt⟩=⟨12sin⁡(2t)+c1,tan⁡(t)+c2⟩.

The initial condition F(π4)=⟨1,0⟩ gives

F(π4)=⟨12sin⁡(π2)+c1,tan⁡(π4)+c2⟩=⟨1,0⟩⟨12+c1,1+c2⟩=⟨1,0⟩.

Therefore, c1=12 and c2=−1. Consequently

F(t)=⟨12sin⁡(2t)+12,tan⁡(t)−1⟩.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Antiderivative of a Vector-Valued Function That Satisfies a Given Initial Condition
content.worked_solution:
First, we note that 

$$
F(t)=\int {F}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t=\int ⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,,{sec}^{2}⁡(t)⟩\text{d}t.
$$

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,,{sec}^{2}⁡(t)⟩\text{d}t & =⟨\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t,\int {sec}^{2}⁡(t)\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+{c}_{1},\,\operatorname{tan}⁡(t)+{c}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

The initial condition $F(\frac{\pi }{4})=⟨1,\,0⟩$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}F(\frac{\pi }{4})=⟨\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+{c}_{1},\,\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})+{c}_{2}⟩ & =⟨1,\,0⟩ \\ ⟨\frac{1}{2}+{c}_{1},\,1+{c}_{2}⟩ & =⟨1,\,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${c}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}$ and ${c}_{2}=-1.$ Consequently

$$
F(t)=⟨\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+\frac{1}{2},\,\operatorname{tan}⁡(t)-1⟩.
$$
